prize_parts.citation: for the optical lattice clock, from the magic-wavelength concept that allows many atoms to be interrogated free of Doppler and recoil shifts to fractional uncertainties at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B015 as a single-part prize to Katori and Ye. After the first round I can state in one sentence what is new relative to the 2005 and 2012 prizes. Hall and Haensch gave us the comb that counts optical cycles, and Wineland and Haroche showed how to control and measure a single quantum system. The lattice clock does something neither did: at the magic wavelength the light shifts of the two clock levels cancel by design, so thousands of atoms can be held and read out in parallel with Doppler and recoil effects removed, which attacks the signal-to-noise limit statistically rather than through one ion. That is the new principle, and it is why the 10^-18 regime became reachable. The maturity evidence is what I trust most: independent clocks at JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST and SYRTE agree at that level in direct comparisons, and the same clocks have already been used as instruments on nature, for gravitational redshift across millimetres and for bounds on drifting constants. The credit is a clean pair, there is no collaboration-scale problem, and the field has no recent prize of its own. Every member who does not prefer B015 has said they would support it or not oppose it, so it is also the configuration least likely to be unfair to anyone's scientific judgment. I do not want to claim consensus as a reason, but it is a fair check that the physics survives the objections raised against it.
statement.case_against: The reservations from round 1 remain and I do not dismiss them. This is a very large step in precision and a new scheme, but it is not the discovery of a new phenomenon in the sense that twisted bilayer graphene or topological insulators are, and a committee that weights new phenomena above new instruments could reasonably prefer those. The redefinition of the second has not happened, and I do not think it should appear in the citation or count as evidence. The credit to Katori and Ye alone leaves out Lemonde and the Paris group, Pfau, Lemke and Ludlow, and the NIST and PTB teams, who made lattice clocks work in practice. I cannot show from my own files that the early NIST and PTB demonstrations are adequately recognised by a two-name credit, and I would welcome an external reviewer on exactly this point.

responses.point: Stefan asked how the citation can name the lattice scheme and the 10^-18 performance so that it does not claim the comb or the ion clock, and asked whether the credit to NIST and PTB is understated.
responses.response: The wording I propose is the one in my citation: it names the magic-wavelength concept and the many-atom, Doppler- and recoil-free interrogation, and then the 10^-18 level, and it makes no mention of the comb, of single ions or of the second. On the second question I think we agree that I cannot settle it from here. My answer as a theorist is that the decisive conceptual step, the magic-wavelength condition with a neutral-atom lattice, is Katori's, and the decisive demonstration that it reaches 10^-18 and can be used on nature is Ye's. The groups at NIST, PTB, SYRTE and elsewhere made essential refinements, such as blackbody control and comparison links, but I do not see a third name whose contribution is on the same footing. I note your Boulder tie to the Hall tradition and I think it is properly disclosed; it is a lineage, not a bearing on the credit.

responses.point: Bernhard says the new element is the magic-wavelength trapping scheme and many-atom interrogation, wants the citation to name the mechanism, and wants the redefinition of the second kept out and the fundamental-physics payoff treated cautiously.
responses.response: I accept all three of his points and have changed my citation to follow them. In round 1 I leaned a little on the redshift and constants tests; I now agree that a prize must rest on what has been demonstrated, and the demonstrations I would cite are the inter-laboratory agreement at 10^-18 and the millimetre-scale redshift measurement, which has been done, not the redefinition or dark-matter searches, which have not. I also take his worry that B015 may be strong simply because it is the safe choice. That is why I tested it against the lineage argument again rather than relying on the support count, and I find that the argument holds up: the many-atom lattice is a different mechanism from the single-ion route.

responses.point: Olle holds B051 as his preference, accepts that B015 reproducibility is real, and says he would support B015 if the topological insulator credit cannot be resolved.
responses.response: I understand why the discovery of a new state of matter is the stronger kind of merit, and I do not think precision measurement outranks it automatically. But you have yourself named the weak point: Mele is a co-originator of Kane-Mele, Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed the HgTe system, and a trio drawn from the three-name limit must leave out someone decisive. Mehlig's trio and yours differ for exactly that reason, and I do not see how the committee can defend either without more expert input. Measured against that, a pair of names whose contributions nobody disputes is the more defensible choice. On lineage, we still differ on whether the lattice is a new principle, but I think the many-atom statistical argument answers the 'only better precision' objection.

responses.point: Eva Olsson prefers B017 for a new phenomenon opened by theory and experiment, accepts that the mechanism is unresolved, and says she would not oppose B015 if the committee prefers a metrology prize and the citation names the invention.
responses.response: I agree with your condition: the citation should name the invention, the lattice clock, and its operating principle, not only the number. I have written it that way. On B017 I share your admiration for a single tunable angle producing correlated states, and the Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction followed by experiment is a clean structure. My hesitation is the one you and Mehlig both state: we do not yet know why the superconductivity appears, and twist-angle disorder still affects sample reproducibility. A prize for B017 in a few years, when the mechanism is clearer, would not seem early to me; today I judge the clock to be further along in understanding.

responses.point: Mark, as chair, asked whether B040 can be credited defensibly within three names, and whether the committee wants a second part at all.
responses.response: On B040 I defer to you and Danielsson on the physics, but I have not seen anything that resolves the credit: the diffuse flux is firm, source identifications are still developing, and the AMANDA, Baikal and ANTARES history makes a single name fragile. On a second part, my answer is no. B015 uses two of the three permitted names, so only a one-person part could be added, and I do not see a shortlisted entry that is both a single-name credit and defensible. I do not think a second part should be added for balance alone; a single, well-argued part is better than a weak pairing, and the first-round supporters of B040 have themselves said it is not ready.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the magic-wavelength lattice with many-atom interrogation as a new principle distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes, or sees it as a large quantitative step.

Whether naming only Katori and Ye fairly reflects the contributions of Lemonde, Pfau, Lemke, Ludlow and the NIST, PTB and SYRTE groups; an external reviewer on the early lattice-clock demonstrations would help.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second argues for waiting a year. I think not, and I would keep it out of the citation, but the timing is a judgment and not a physical fact.
Whether a precision measurement satisfies the statutory emphasis on discovery or invention as strongly as a new phenomenon such as B017 or B051 would.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict with Katori, Ye or the other credited names. I have no direct collaboration with them. I remain a long-time close collaborator of Anne L'Huillier, a 2023 laureate, and have co-authored with Lund and ETH attosecond groups, but no shortlisted entry concerns attosecond physics. My field is atomic many-body theory, adjacent to the clock and cold-atom entries, which is expertise and not a conflict. I note Kroll's disclosed Boulder lineage and Johansson's disclosed ties to circuit QED, neither of which affects my position.
